prompt: A *group* is a set $G$ with a binary operation (written as multiplication, $gh$) such that: (a) it is associative, $(gh)k=g(hk)$; (b) there is an identity element $1$ with $g1=1g=g$ for all $g$; (c) every $g$ has an inverse $g^{-1}$ with $gg^{-1}=g^{-1}g=1$. A group is *abelian* if $gh=hg$ for all $g,h$. Prove that the integers $\mathbb Z$ form an abelian group under addition.
answer: Closed, associative, identity $0$, inverse $-x$, commutative.

solutions.title: Check the axioms
solutions.body: The sum of two integers is an integer; addition is associative; $0$ is the identity since $x+0=0+x=x$; each $x$ has inverse $-x$ since $x+(-x)=(-x)+x=0$. So $\mathbb Z$ is a group, and it is abelian since $x+y=y+x$. $\blacksquare$

answer: No inverses: $1$ has no $x\ge 0$ with $1+x=0$.

solutions.title: Inverses fail
solutions.body: The identity is $0$. But $1$ has no inverse: there is no $x\ge0$ with $1+x=0$. So axiom (c) fails (the same holds for every nonzero element).

solutions.title: Inverses fail

Prove that the identity of a group is unique, and that every element has a unique inverse: if $1$ and $1'$ are identities then $1=1'$, and if $a$ and $b$ are inverses of $g$ then $a=b$.

solutions.title: Compare two candidates
solutions.body:
If $1,1'$ are identities: $1=1\cdot1'$ (as $1'$ is an identity) and $1\cdot1'=1'$ (as $1$ is an identity), so $1=1'$.

If $a,b$ are both inverses of $g$: $a=a1=a(gb)=(ag)b=1b=b$. $\blacksquare$

A group is *abelian* if $gh=hg$ for all $g,h$. Prove the cancellation laws: if $gh=gk$ then $h=k$, and if $gk=hk$ then $g=h$. Conclude that if $gh=g$ or $hg=g$, then $h=1$.
answer: Multiply by $g^{-1}$ on the left (resp. $k^{-1}$ on the right).

solutions.title: Multiply by inverses
solutions.body:
If $gh=gk$, multiply on the left by $g^{-1}$: $h=g^{-1}gh=g^{-1}gk=k$. If $gk=hk$, multiply on the right by $k^{-1}$: $g=h$.

If $gh=g=g1$, the first law gives $h=1$; if $hg=g=1g$, the second law gives $h=1$. $\blacksquare$

The *order* of an element $g$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ with $g^k=1$ ($\infty$ if there is none); the order of a group is its number of elements. Prove that if the group $G$ has finite order, then every element $g\in G$ has finite order.
answer: Powers of $g$ repeat, so $g^{j-i}=1$.

solutions.title: Pigeonhole
solutions.body: Since $G$ is finite, the powers $1,g,g^2,\dots$ cannot all be distinct: $g^i=g^j$ for some $0\le i<j$. Multiplying by $g^{-i}$ gives $g^{j-i}=1$ with $j-i>0$, so $g$ has finite order. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Multiply
solutions.body: $g\cdot g^{n-1}=g^n=1$ and $g^{n-1}g=g^n=1$, so $g^{n-1}$ is an inverse of $g$, and by uniqueness equals $g^{-1}$. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Division algorithm
solutions.body: Let $m$ be the order of $g$ and write $k=qm+r$ with $0\le r<m$. Then $1=g^k=(g^m)^qg^r=g^r$. If $r>0$ this contradicts the minimality of $m$, so $r=0$ and $m\mid k$. $\blacksquare$

Consider a regular pentagonal pyramid. Describe the elements of its (rotational) symmetry group, i.e. the group of rotations that leave the pyramid looking unchanged.
answer: The five rotations by $0^\circ,72^\circ,144^\circ,216^\circ,288^\circ$ about the axis through the apex and the center of the base.

solutions.title: Describe the rotations
solutions.body: A rotation symmetry must fix the apex (the only vertex where five triangular faces meet), hence fixes the axis from the apex to the center of the base, and is a rotation about this axis. It must map the regular pentagonal base to itself, so the angle is a multiple of $72^\circ$. The group has the five elements: clockwise rotations by $0^\circ,72^\circ,144^\circ,216^\circ,288^\circ$ about that axis.

answer: Generated by the $72^\circ$ rotation.

solutions.title: Find a generator
solutions.body: Let $\rho$ be the clockwise rotation by $72^\circ$. Then $\rho^k$ is the rotation by $72k^\circ$, so $\rho^0,\rho,\rho^2,\rho^3,\rho^4$ are exactly the five rotations. Hence the group is cyclic with generator $\rho$. $\blacksquare$

answer: Rotation by $72k^\circ\leftrightarrow k\bmod5$.

solutions.title: Match rotations with residues
solutions.body: Associate the rotation by $72k^\circ$ with $k\bmod5$. This is a bijection between the five rotations and $\mathbb Z/5$. Applying the rotation by $72j^\circ$ and then by $72k^\circ$ gives the rotation by $72(j+k)^\circ$, which corresponds to $j+k\bmod5$ (as $360^\circ$ is the identity). So composition corresponds to addition mod $5$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: A *group* is a set $G$ with a binary operation (written as multiplication, $gh$) such that: (a) it is associative, $(gh)k=g(hk)$; (b) there is an identity element $1$ with $g1=1g=g$ for all $g$; (c) every $g$ has an inverse $g^{-1}$ with $gg^{-1}=g^{-1}g=1$. A group is *abelian* if $gh=hg$ for all $g,h$. For $g$ in a group, $g^k$ is $g$ multiplied by itself $k$ times, $g^0=1$, $g^{-k}=(g^{-1})^k$. The *order* of an element $g$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ with $g^k=1$ ($\infty$ if there is none); the order of a group is its number of elements. A group $C$ is *cyclic* if there is an element $g$ (a *generator*) such that every element of $C$ is $g^k$ for some integer $k$. Let $C_n$ be the cyclic group generated by an element $g$ of order $n$. Show that the elements of $C_n$ are exactly $\{1,g,g^2,\dots,g^{n-1}\}$, and that these are distinct.
answer: Division algorithm; distinctness by minimality of the order.

solutions.title: Reduce exponents
solutions.body:
Every element is $g^k$; write $k=qn+r$ with $0\le r<n$; then $g^k=(g^n)^qg^r=g^r$. So every element is in the list.

Distinct: if $g^i=g^j$ with $0\le i<j\le n-1$ then $g^{j-i}=1$ with $0<j-i<n$, contradicting that $n$ is the order of $g$. Hence $C_n$ has exactly $n$ elements. $\blacksquare$

prompt: A *group* is a set $G$ with a binary operation (written as multiplication, $gh$) such that: (a) it is associative, $(gh)k=g(hk)$; (b) there is an identity element $1$ with $g1=1g=g$ for all $g$; (c) every $g$ has an inverse $g^{-1}$ with $gg^{-1}=g^{-1}g=1$. A group is *abelian* if $gh=hg$ for all $g,h$. For $g$ in a group, $g^k$ is $g$ multiplied by itself $k$ times, $g^0=1$, $g^{-k}=(g^{-1})^k$. The *order* of an element $g$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ with $g^k=1$ ($\infty$ if there is none); the order of a group is its number of elements. A group $C$ is *cyclic* if there is an element $g$ (a *generator*) such that every element of $C$ is $g^k$ for some integer $k$. Let $C_n$ be the cyclic group generated by an element $g$ of order $n$. What is the order of $g^k$ in terms of $k$ and $n$? Given this, what must be true of $k$ and $n$ for $g^k$ to be a (another) generator of $C_n$?
answer: The order of $g^k$ is $\dfrac{n}{\gcd(k,n)}$; $g^k$ is a generator iff $\gcd(k,n)=1$.

solutions.title: Compute the order
solutions.body:
Let $d=\gcd(k,n)$, $a=n/d$, $b=k/d$ (coprime). Then $(g^k)^a=(g^n)^b=1$, so the order $m$ of $g^k$ divides $a$ (by the previous result: order divides any exponent giving the identity). Conversely $g^{km}=1$ implies $n\mid km$, i.e. $ad\mid bdm$, so $a\mid bm$ and since $\gcd(a,b)=1$, $a\mid m$. Hence $m=a=\frac n{\gcd(k,n)}$.

$g^k$ generates $C_n$ iff its order is $n$ (it then has $n$ distinct powers), i.e. iff $\gcd(k,n)=1$. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Apply $r$ then $s$
solutions.body:
Start: $1$ at the top, $2$ at the bottom right, $3$ at the bottom left (clockwise order).

After $r$ (clockwise $120^\circ$ moves every label to the next corner clockwise): $3$ at the top, $1$ at the bottom right, $2$ at the bottom left.

Then $s$ (swap the two bottom corners, keep the top): $3$ at the top, $2$ at the bottom right, $1$ at the bottom left.

**Answer: top $3$, bottom right $2$, bottom left $1$.**

prompt: A *symmetry operation* of an object is a rotation, reflection or combination of both that keeps the object looking the same; these form a group under composition, where $\sigma\tau$ means: first apply $\tau$, then $\sigma$ (products are read right to left). The dihedral group $D_{2n}$ is the group of symmetries (rotations and reflections) of a regular $n$-gon; it has $2n$ elements. Let $r$ be clockwise rotation by $\frac{360}{n}$ degrees and $s$ a reflection across a fixed axis; $r$ has order $n$, $s$ has order $2$, and $r,s$ generate $D_{2n}$. Prove that $sr^k$ has order $2$ for all $0\le k\le n-1$, and conclude that $sr^k=r^{-k}s$.
answer: $sr^k$ is a reflection, hence of order $2$, hence its own inverse $r^{-k}s$.

solutions.title: Reflections have order 2
solutions.body:
$r^k$ preserves orientation and $s$ reverses it, so the symmetry $sr^k$ of the $n$-gon reverses orientation and fixes the center. An orientation-reversing isometry fixing a point is a reflection across a line through that point, and applying a reflection twice gives the identity. So $(sr^k)^2=1$, i.e. $sr^k$ has order $2$ (it is not the identity, being orientation-reversing).

Therefore $sr^k=(sr^k)^{-1}=(r^k)^{-1}s^{-1}=r^{-k}s$ using $s^{-1}=s$. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Compare $sr$ and $rs$

$1\to4\to2\to3$; $3\to3\to4\to4$; $4\to2\to3\to1$; $2\to1\to1\to2$.

A permutation can be written in cycle notation as a product of disjoint cycles, e.g. $(1\,2\,3)$ sends $1\to2\to3\to1$; $(1\,2)$ is a *transposition*; the identity is written $1$. The *order* of an element $g$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ with $g^k=1$ ($\infty$ if there is none); the order of a group is its number of elements. Show that, when written as a product of disjoint cycles, the order of an element of a symmetric group is the least common multiple of the lengths of its cycles. (You may assume disjoint cycles commute.)
answer: A cycle of length $m$ has order $m$; powers of disjoint cycles do not interact.

solutions.title: Order of a cycle, then lcm
solutions.body:
A cycle of length $m$ moves each of its entries by one step around the cycle, so its $k$th power fixes an entry iff $m\mid k$; hence it has order $m$.

Let $\sigma=c_1\cdots c_t$ with disjoint cycles of lengths $m_1,\dots,m_t$. Since they commute, $\sigma^k=c_1^k\cdots c_t^k$, and the factors act on disjoint sets, so $\sigma^k=1$ iff every $c_i^k=1$, i.e. iff $m_i\mid k$ for all $i$. The least such $k$ is $\operatorname{lcm}(m_1,\dots,m_t)$. $\blacksquare$

answer: Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles and $(a_1\,a_2\,\dots\,a_m)=(a_1\,a_2)(a_2\,a_3)\cdots(a_{m-1}\,a_m)$.

solutions.title: Cycles are products of transpositions
solutions.body: Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles (follow each element until it returns), so it suffices to write a cycle as a product of transpositions. We claim $(a_1\,a_2\,\dots\,a_m)=(a_1\,a_2)(a_2\,a_3)\cdots(a_{m-1}\,a_m)$. Read right to left: $a_m$ is moved to $a_{m-1}$ by the last factor, then to $a_{m-2}$, ..., reaching $a_1$ after the last transposition, so $a_m\mapsto a_1$. For $i<m$, $a_i$ is untouched by the factors $(a_j\,a_{j+1})$ with $j>i$, then $(a_{i}\,a_{i+1})$ sends it to $a_{i+1}$, and later factors (those with $j<i$) fix $a_{i+1}$. So $a_i\mapsto a_{i+1}$, as in the cycle. (A cycle of length $1$ is the identity, the empty product.) $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: $S_n$ is the group of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ under composition (applied right to left). A permutation can be written in cycle notation as a product of disjoint cycles, e.g. $(1\,2\,3)$ sends $1\to2\to3\to1$; $(1\,2)$ is a *transposition*; the identity is written $1$. $A_n$ is the group of *even* permutations in $S_n$: those that can be written as a product of an even number of transpositions (odd permutations use an odd number). Prove that a permutation $\sigma$ in $S_n$ cannot be both even and odd: it cannot be written both as a product of an even number of transpositions and as a product of an odd number of transpositions.
answer: The parity of the number of inversions changes with every transposition.

solutions.title: Count inversions
solutions.body:
For a permutation $\sigma$ (viewed as the sequence $\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n)$) let $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)$ be the number of pairs $i<j$ with $\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$. Multiplying on the right by a transposition $\tau=(a\,b)$ swaps the entries in positions $a$ and $b$.

*Adjacent swap* ($b=a+1$): the relative order of the two swapped entries flips and every other pair keeps its relative order, so $\operatorname{inv}$ changes by exactly $\pm1$.

*General swap* ($a<b$): swapping positions $a,b$ equals $2(b-a)-1$ adjacent swaps (move the entry at $a$ to position $b$ by $b-a$ adjacent swaps, then move the entry now at $b-1$ to position $a$ by $b-a-1$ adjacent swaps). That is an odd number, so $\operatorname{inv}$ changes parity.

If $\sigma=\tau_1\cdots\tau_k$ then starting from the identity ($\operatorname{inv}=0$) and multiplying on the right by $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k$ in turn, $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)\equiv k\pmod 2$. Hence the parity of the number of transpositions equals the parity of $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)$ and is determined by $\sigma$. In particular the identity ($\operatorname{inv}=0$) is even and not odd. $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: $S_n$ is the group of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ under composition (applied right to left). A permutation can be written in cycle notation as a product of disjoint cycles, e.g. $(1\,2\,3)$ sends $1\to2\to3\to1$; $(1\,2)$ is a *transposition*; the identity is written $1$. $A_n$ is the group of *even* permutations in $S_n$: those that can be written as a product of an even number of transpositions (odd permutations use an odd number). You may use that no permutation is both even and odd. Prove that the product of two even or of two odd permutations is even, while the product of an even and an odd permutation is odd. Conclude that $A_n$ has order $\frac{n!}{2}$ for $n>1$.
answer: Parities add; multiplication by $(1\,2)$ is a bijection from even to odd permutations.

solutions.title: Parities add
solutions.body:
Writing each factor as a product of transpositions and concatenating the lists, the number of transpositions of the product is the sum of the two numbers. Even$+$even and odd$+$odd are even; even$+$odd is odd. By the previous result the parity is well defined.

For $n>1$ let $\tau=(1\,2)$ (odd). The map $\sigma\mapsto\tau\sigma$ sends even permutations to odd ones and odd to even ones, and it is its own inverse, so it is a bijection between the even and the odd permutations. Hence they are equally numerous: $|A_n|=\frac{n!}2$. $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: $S_n$ is the group of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ under composition (applied right to left). A permutation can be written in cycle notation as a product of disjoint cycles, e.g. $(1\,2\,3)$ sends $1\to2\to3\to1$; $(1\,2)$ is a *transposition*; the identity is written $1$. $A_n$ is the group of *even* permutations in $S_n$: those that can be written as a product of an even number of transpositions (odd permutations use an odd number). You may use that parity is well defined. Show that, written in cycle notation, the elements of $A_n$ are exactly the permutations of $S_n$ with an even number of cycles of even length. Use this to list the elements of $A_4$.

solutions.title: Cycles and parity
solutions.body:
A cycle of length $m$ is a product of $m-1$ transpositions: $(a_1\,\dots\,a_m)=(a_1\,a_2)(a_2\,a_3)\cdots(a_{m-1}\,a_m)$. So a permutation with cycles of lengths $m_1,\dots,m_t$ is a product of $\sum(m_i-1)$ transpositions, which is even iff the number of $i$ with $m_i$ even is even.

In $S_4$ the cycle types are: identity ($0$ even cycles: even); transposition ($1$): odd; two disjoint transpositions ($2$): even; $3$-cycle ($0$): even; $4$-cycle ($1$): odd. So $A_4$ consists of the identity, the $3$ products of two disjoint transpositions $(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)$, and the $8$ three-cycles $(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2),(1\,2\,4),(1\,4\,2),(1\,3\,4),(1\,4\,3),(2\,3\,4),(2\,4\,3)$: $12=\frac{4!}2$ elements. $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: $S_n$ is the group of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ under composition (applied right to left). A permutation can be written in cycle notation as a product of disjoint cycles, e.g. $(1\,2\,3)$ sends $1\to2\to3\to1$; $(1\,2)$ is a *transposition*; the identity is written $1$. $A_n$ is the group of *even* permutations in $S_n$: those that can be written as a product of an even number of transpositions (odd permutations use an odd number). Prove that $A_n$ is generated by its $3$-cycles: every even permutation is a product of $3$-cycles.
answer: A product of two transpositions is a product of $3$-cycles.

solutions.title: Pair up the transpositions
solutions.body:
An even permutation is a product of an even number of transpositions; group them in consecutive pairs $(a\,b)(c\,d)$. It suffices to show each pair is a product of $3$-cycles.

- If $\{a,b\}=\{c,d\}$ the pair is the identity (empty product).
- If they share one element, say $(a\,b)(a\,c)$ with $a,b,c$ distinct: right to left, $a\to c$, $c\to b$, $b\to a$, so it equals the $3$-cycle $(a\,c\,b)$.
- If disjoint: $(a\,b)(c\,d)=(a\,b)(b\,c)\cdot(b\,c)(c\,d)$, a product of two $3$-cycles by the previous case (since $(b\,c)(b\,c)=1$). $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A *symmetry operation* of an object is a rotation, reflection or combination of both that keeps the object looking the same; these form a group under composition, where $\sigma\tau$ means: first apply $\tau$, then $\sigma$ (products are read right to left). $A_n$ is the group of *even* permutations in $S_n$: those that can be written as a product of an even number of transpositions (odd permutations use an odd number). The rotation group of a tetrahedron consists of the rotations of $\mathbb R^3$ that map a regular tetrahedron to itself. Prove that this group is equivalent (isomorphic) to $A_4$ by considering its effect on the four vertices and computing its order.
answer: Rotations permute the $4$ vertices faithfully, each such permutation is even, and the group has $12=|A_4|$ elements.

solutions.title: Embed in $S_4$
solutions.body:
A rotation permutes the four vertices, and composition of rotations corresponds to composition of permutations. A rotation fixing all four vertices fixes four non-coplanar points, hence is the identity, so the map to $S_4$ is injective.

Order: a rotation is determined by where it sends a vertex $v$ (4 choices) and then by a rotation about the axis through the image vertex and the opposite face center that preserves the tetrahedron ($3$ choices: angles $0,120^\circ,240^\circ$). So there are $4\cdot3=12$ rotations: the identity, $8$ rotations by $\pm120^\circ$ about axes through a vertex and the opposite face center, and $3$ rotations by $180^\circ$ about axes through midpoints of opposite edges.

Parity: a $120^\circ$ rotation fixes one vertex and cycles the other three, a $3$-cycle (even); a $180^\circ$ rotation swaps two pairs of vertices, a product of two transpositions (even). So the image lies in $A_4$, which has $12$ elements. An injective map from a group of order $12$ into $A_4$ is onto, hence an isomorphism. $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A group $G$ *acts* on a set $S$ if each $g\in G$ gives a function $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ on $S$ with $1\cdot s=s$ and $h\cdot(g\cdot s)=(hg)\cdot s$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $O_s=\{g\cdot s: g\in G\}$ and its *stabilizer* is $G_s=\{g\in G: g\cdot s=s\}$. Show that if $a,b\in S$ and $b=g\cdot a$ for some $g\in G$, then $a=g^{-1}\cdot b$.
answer: $g^{-1}\cdot(g\cdot a)=(g^{-1}g)\cdot a=1\cdot a=a$.

solutions.title: Use the action axioms
solutions.body: $g^{-1}\cdot b=g^{-1}\cdot(g\cdot a)=(g^{-1}g)\cdot a=1\cdot a=a$. $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A group $G$ *acts* on a set $S$ if each $g\in G$ gives a function $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ on $S$ with $1\cdot s=s$ and $h\cdot(g\cdot s)=(hg)\cdot s$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $O_s=\{g\cdot s: g\in G\}$ and its *stabilizer* is $G_s=\{g\in G: g\cdot s=s\}$. The rotation group of the cube acts on the set of centers of its faces. Find the number of elements in the orbit and in the stabilizer of the center of one face.
answer: Orbit: $6$ elements; stabilizer: $4$ elements.

solutions.title: Count
solutions.body:
Orbit: a $90^\circ$ rotation about a horizontal axis takes the center of the top face to the center of any adjacent face and a $180^\circ$ rotation takes it to the opposite face, so every one of the $6$ face centers is reached (orbit size $6$).

Stabilizer: a rotation fixing the center of a face fixes the axis through that point and the center of the cube, so it is a rotation about this axis. It must map the cube to itself: only the angles $0^\circ,90^\circ,180^\circ,270^\circ$ work. So the stabilizer has $4$ elements.

**Answer: orbit $6$, stabilizer $4$.**

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A group $G$ *acts* on a set $S$ if each $g\in G$ gives a function $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ on $S$ with $1\cdot s=s$ and $h\cdot(g\cdot s)=(hg)\cdot s$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $O_s=\{g\cdot s: g\in G\}$ and its *stabilizer* is $G_s=\{g\in G: g\cdot s=s\}$. The rotation group of the regular octahedron acts on the midpoints of its edges. Find the number of elements in the orbit and in the stabilizer of the midpoint of one edge.
answer: Orbit: $12$ elements; stabilizer: $2$ elements.

solutions.title: Count
solutions.body:
Take the octahedron with vertices $(\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1)$. Its edge midpoints are the $12$ points $(\pm\frac12,\pm\frac12,0)$ and permutations of coordinates. Rotations by $90^\circ$ about the coordinate axes and cyclic coordinate permutations (rotations by $120^\circ$ about $(1,1,1)$) map any such midpoint to any other, so the orbit has all $12$ elements.

Stabilizer of $m=(\frac12,\frac12,0)$: a rotation fixing $m$ fixes the line through the center and $m$ pointwise, so it is a rotation about the axis $(1,1,0)$. The $180^\circ$ rotation about this axis swaps $(1,0,0)\leftrightarrow(0,1,0)$ and $(0,0,1)\leftrightarrow(0,0,-1)$, a symmetry; other nonzero angles do not map the vertices to vertices. So the stabilizer has $2$ elements.

**Answer: orbit $12$, stabilizer $2$.**

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A group $G$ *acts* on a set $S$ if each $g\in G$ gives a function $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ on $S$ with $1\cdot s=s$ and $h\cdot(g\cdot s)=(hg)\cdot s$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $O_s=\{g\cdot s: g\in G\}$ and its *stabilizer* is $G_s=\{g\in G: g\cdot s=s\}$. (Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem.) Prove that if a finite group $G$ acts on a set $S$ and $s\in S$, then $|G|=|O_s|\cdot|G_s|$.
answer: The map $g\mapsto g\cdot s$ is onto $O_s$ and its fibres are the cosets $hG_s$, each of size $|G_s|$.

solutions.title: Count fibres of the orbit map
solutions.body:
Define $\varphi:G\to O_s$, $\varphi(g)=g\cdot s$; it is onto by definition of $O_s$.

For $g,h\in G$: $\varphi(g)=\varphi(h)\iff g\cdot s=h\cdot s\iff (h^{-1}g)\cdot s=s\iff h^{-1}g\in G_s\iff g\in hG_s$, where $hG_s=\{hx:x\in G_s\}$. (Here we used $h^{-1}\cdot(h\cdot s)=s$ from the action axioms.)

So the fibre of $\varphi$ over $h\cdot s$ is exactly $hG_s$. The map $x\mapsto hx$ is injective (cancellation law), so $|hG_s|=|G_s|$. The fibres partition $G$ into $|O_s|$ sets of size $|G_s|$ each, so $|G|=|O_s|\,|G_s|$. $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A group $G$ *acts* on a set $S$ if each $g\in G$ gives a function $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ on $S$ with $1\cdot s=s$ and $h\cdot(g\cdot s)=(hg)\cdot s$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $O_s=\{g\cdot s: g\in G\}$ and its *stabilizer* is $G_s=\{g\in G: g\cdot s=s\}$. The rotation group of the cube acts on the cube and the rotation group of the regular octahedron acts on the octahedron. Use the Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem and the facts that a face center of a cube has orbit size $6$ and stabilizer size $4$, and an edge midpoint of an octahedron has orbit size $12$ and stabilizer size $2$, to find the order of the cubic and octahedral rotation groups. Also prove that both rotation groups are equivalent (isomorphic) to $S_4$ by finding a set of $4$ objects that is completely permuted by each group.
answer: Both groups have order $24$ and are isomorphic to $S_4$: the cubic group permutes the $4$ space diagonals of the cube; the octahedral group permutes the $4$ pairs of opposite faces of the octahedron.

solutions.title: Order and the action on diagonals
solutions.body:
Orders: cube: $6\cdot4=24$; octahedron: $12\cdot2=24$.

Cube: the four space diagonals (lines through opposite vertices) are permuted by every rotation, giving a homomorphism $\psi:G\to S_4$. Kernel: if a rotation maps every diagonal to itself, then it maps each vertex to itself or to its antipode. If it fixes some vertex $v$, it is a rotation about the diagonal through $v$, by $0^\circ$ or $\pm120^\circ$; a $120^\circ$ rotation cyclically permutes the other three diagonals, which is not allowed, so it is the identity. Otherwise it maps every vertex to its antipode, i.e. $x\mapsto-x$, which reverses orientation and is not a rotation. So the kernel is trivial and $\psi$ is injective; since $|G|=24=|S_4|$, $\psi$ is an isomorphism.

Octahedron: the centers of its $8$ faces are the vertices of a cube, so its rotations are exactly the rotations of that cube (a rotation preserves the octahedron iff it preserves the set of its face centers). The four pairs of opposite faces of the octahedron correspond to the four space diagonals of this cube, so the octahedral group acts faithfully on these four pairs by the same argument and is isomorphic to $S_4$. $\blacksquare$

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A group $G$ *acts* on a set $S$ if each $g\in G$ gives a function $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ on $S$ with $1\cdot s=s$ and $h\cdot(g\cdot s)=(hg)\cdot s$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $O_s=\{g\cdot s: g\in G\}$ and its *stabilizer* is $G_s=\{g\in G: g\cdot s=s\}$. The icosahedron has $12$ vertices; its rotation group acts transitively on the vertices (any vertex can be rotated onto any other), and the rotations fixing a vertex are those about the axis through it that preserve the five triangles meeting there. Use the Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem to determine the order of the icosahedral rotation group (which equals the dodecahedral one).

solutions.title: Orbit-Stabilizer on vertices
solutions.body:
The orbit of a vertex is all $12$ vertices. The stabilizer of a vertex consists of the rotations about the axis through that vertex and the opposite vertex which map the icosahedron to itself; five triangles meet at a vertex, so the angles are multiples of $72^\circ$: $5$ rotations.

By Orbit-Stabilizer, $|G|=12\cdot5=60$.

**Answer: 60**

solutions.title: Using the dodecahedron
solutions.body:
The dodecahedron's group is the same. Its $12$ pentagonal faces form one orbit and the stabilizer of a face is the $5$ rotations about its axis: $12\cdot5=60$. (Alternatively $20$ vertices $\times\,3=60$.)

**Answer: 60**

source.paper: 2014 Power Round (Symmetry Groups of Regular Polyhedra)

prompt: A group $G$ *acts* on a set $S$ if each $g\in G$ gives a function $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ on $S$ with $1\cdot s=s$ and $h\cdot(g\cdot s)=(hg)\cdot s$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $O_s=\{g\cdot s: g\in G\}$ and its *stabilizer* is $G_s=\{g\in G: g\cdot s=s\}$. $A_n$ is the group of *even* permutations in $S_n$: those that can be written as a product of an even number of transpositions (odd permutations use an odd number). As shown in the figure, a cube can be inscribed in a dodecahedron by drawing diagonals of the pentagonal faces (one diagonal in each of the $12$ faces). Drawing all $5$ diagonals of all $12$ pentagonal faces gives $5$ cubes inscribed in the dodecahedron, each diagonal belonging to exactly one cube. The rotation group $G$ of the dodecahedron has order $60$ (and permutes these cubes). Show that every even permutation of the $5$ cubes is achieved by some rotation and, combined with the order of the group, conclude that the dodecahedral (and thus the icosahedral) rotation group is equivalent (isomorphic) to $A_5$.
answer: The action of $G$ on the $5$ cubes is an injective homomorphism $G\to S_5$; its image has order $60$, so it is the index-$2$ subgroup $A_5$.

solutions.title: Action on the five cubes
solutions.body:
Every rotation of $G$ maps the set of $60$ face diagonals to itself, so it permutes the $5$ cubes (each cube consists of $12$ diagonals, one per face). This gives a homomorphism $\psi:G\to S_5$.

*Transitivity and stabilizer size.* The $72^\circ$ rotation about the axis through a face center cycles the five diagonals of that face; they lie in five different cubes (a cube uses one diagonal per face), so $G$ is transitive on the cubes and contains an element acting as a $5$-cycle. By Orbit-Stabilizer, the stabilizer $H$ of a cube has order $60/5=12$.

*$\psi$ is injective.* Let $K=\ker\psi$, a normal subgroup contained in $H$, so $|K|\le12$ and $5\nmid|K|$. $G$ consists of the identity, $24$ rotations of order $5$ (about the $6$ face axes), $20$ of order $3$ (about the $10$ vertex axes) and $15$ of order $2$ (about the $15$ edge axes). If $K$ contained a rotation $g$ of order $3$, it would contain all its conjugates; the elements commuting with $g$ preserve its axis and cannot reverse it (a reversing rotation inverts $g$), so they are the $3$ rotations about that axis. Hence $g$ has $60/3=20$ conjugates, more than $12$, a contradiction. If $K$ contained an involution $h$, the elements commuting with $h$ preserve its axis, whose stabilizer in $G$ has order $60/15=4$, so $h$ has at least $15>12$ conjugates, again a contradiction. Thus $K=\{1\}$ and $\psi$ is injective.

*Image is $A_5$.* The image $\psi(G)$ is a subgroup of $S_5$ of order $60$, so of index $2$. For any $\sigma\in S_5$, $\sigma^2\in\psi(G)$ (the quotient by an index-$2$ subgroup has order $2$). Every $3$-cycle $c$ satisfies $c=(c^2)^2$ (because $c^4=c$), so every $3$-cycle lies in $\psi(G)$. The $3$-cycles generate $A_5$ (previous results), so $A_5\subseteq\psi(G)$, and both have order $60$: $\psi(G)=A_5$. In particular every even permutation of the five cubes is realised by a (unique) rotation, and $G\cong A_5$. $\blacksquare$
